extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, scientific method, and the moral/social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for reasoning, identifying fallacies, and adapting scientific methods to the study of mind and society; includes definitions of fallacies, methodological prescriptions, and cautions about terminology and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio Principii (begging the question)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument that assumes the point in dispute by making a premise that is really identical with the conclusion (e.g. asserting that justice and wisdom 'must be something' when the intended sense of 'something' differs between premise and conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when a premise covertly restates the conclusion or assumes what it should prove; watch for equivocation of terms (ambiguous middle-term) where the same word is used in different senses across premise and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy from A priori/prejudice about conceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that because something cannot be conceived by the imagination it cannot exist (the 'a priori' fallacy or natural prejudice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arguments that appeal to the limitations of imagination (example: using inability to conceive a minimum thickness to 'prove' infinite divisibility). Test whether the premise actually adds anything beyond the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden underlying fallacy diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Many fallacies of verbal confusion are manifestations of some other deductive or ratiocinative fallacy lurking beneath the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with a verbal juggle, search for the deeper fallacy (misapplied inference, illicit assumption, equivocation) that gives it plausibility; clearing the verbal confusion will usually expose the substantive error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require proof for premises as much as for conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat a premise as self-evident merely because it makes the conclusion seem plausible (example: Euler’s algebraic argument that minus×minus cannot give minus assumes without proof that a product must differ when one factor sign changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize and demand justification for premises, especially when they underlie traditionally accepted operations; seek more comprehensive conceptual analyses rather than relying on superficial plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular standards in ethics (circular moral justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking 'natural or instinctive sentiments' as the standard of moral truth and then dismissing dissenters as 'unhealthy' is circular (defining the standard by its supposed universal acceptance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing normative standards, do not bootstrap the standard by labelling disagreement as aberration; provide independent justification rather than explaining exceptions away by impugning dissenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid social-contract circularity (question-begging justifications of obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deriving the obligation to obey sovereigns from a supposed ancestral promise (social compact) begs the question — it assumes the binding force of promises made by others without grounding why we are bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand an ultimate ground for obligations (e.g., social utility, consequences) rather than relying on hypothetical or fictitious historical acts; examine whether the purported justification truly explains bindingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoratio Elenchi (irrelevant conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting some other proposition for the one that requires proof — proving something that may be emotionally or practically similar but is not the proposition at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the argument establishes precisely the contested proposition; beware of rhetorical moves (evoking emotions, attacking associated categories) that achieve 'practical' acceptance without proving the target claim. Examples include proving that a fraud is atrocious rather than proving the accused committed fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper appeal to passions / extraneous matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Using emotional appeals or extraneous features to sway judgment instead of addressing the question (Aristotle’s ἔξω τοῦ πράγματος — things outside the matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and discount arguments that rely on excitement of emotion, name-calling, or irrelevancies; focus on evidence and direct relevance to the proposition under dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proving the class instead of the instance
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving that a class-of-cases has a property (e.g., that frauds are atrocious) does not by itself prove that a particular instance has been shown to be such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish universal/class claims from particular/instance claims; do not accept class-labeling as a substitute for proving facts about the specific case under discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate targetting of claims in refutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutations must engage the actual claim made (e.g., Malthus’s claim is not that population always increases at a fixed ratio but that, absent restraints, it tends to increase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid straw man or mischaracterized refutations that attack a caricature rather than the author's explicit thesis; read claims in context and respond to their stated scope and qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect distinctions of levels of explanation (phenomenon vs noumenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not refute a metaphysical denial of substance (Berkeley's denial of matter as substratum) by appealing to sensory appearances — the skeptic's claim concerns a hidden cause, not the sensations themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether the dispute is about appearances, their causes, or metaphysical substrata; apply evidence appropriate to the level of the claim rather than attacking an irrelevant manifestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of evidence and method must be empirical, not purely a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of our rational faculty and theories of method are learned by observing the agent at work; they should not be constructed purely a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive methodological rules from the history and practice of successful inquiry (learn to do difficult things by generalizing from simpler cases); avoid inventing procedures divorced from observed effective practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize method from simpler to more complex sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The way of obtaining truth is first seen by superior minds in comparatively simple cases and then adapted by judicious generalization to more complex ones (use simpler scientific achievements as exemplars for moral/social inquiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing methods for moral and social sciences, identify which procedures worked in established natural sciences and adapt them where appropriate; recognize peculiar difficulties peculiar to the study of man and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether human actions are governed by invariable laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Before treating conduct as the subject of science, inquire whether the constancy of causation that grounds scientific theory obtains among human actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine empirical regularities in behavior; evaluate to what degree predictability and regular succession of antecedents/consequents exist in human affairs and whether they permit scientific treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition clarity: philosophical necessity vs common 'necessity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical Necessity (that actions would be inferable given motives and character) must be distinguished from everyday sense of 'necessity' (irresistibleness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misleading terminology — do not let the ordinary sense of 'necessity' (implying irresistibleness) distort understanding of causal predictability. Prefer precise expressions of causation and predictability over evocative but ambiguous words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fatalistic misconstruals of determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Believing actions are determined by causes need not imply helplessness or the futility of self-effort; misconstruing determinism as fatalism is a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between predictability from known antecedents and the practical possibility of changing antecedents; recognize that agents can influence their circumstances and thereby alter future conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize agents' capacity for self-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although character is formed by organization, education, and circumstances, individuals have power to alter their character by willing the requisite means — the desire to change is itself a causal circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral-scientific analysis, incorporate feedback where agents' volitions and efforts become causes that reshape character; avoid treating character as wholly fixed and exogenous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden account of motives beyond anticipatory pleasure/pain
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'motive' is not always or solely the anticipation of pleasure or pain; through association actions can become desired for their own sake and continue even when no pleasure is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or explaining human behavior, include habit, association, and the internalization of actions as ends; do not reduce all volitions to simple utilitarian calculus without empirical support.
